meta.source: CSTA K-12 Computer Science Standards, 2026 revision
meta.shape_note: Extraction covers the 45 core 'Middle School' (grades 6-8) standards and the 46 core 'High School' standards, across the same 5 concepts (Algorithms & Design, Programming, Data & Analysis, Systems & Security, Computing & Society) at each level -- the two bands share concept/subconcept names but are distinct standards, not the same code repeated. The CSTA 2026 revision also defines an Elementary band (PK-5, more granular, one standard set per grade) and two elective High School specialization tiers, 'Specialty I' (73 standards) and 'Specialty II' (62 standards), covering Data Science, Cybersecurity, Artificial Intelligence, Game Development, Software Development, Physical Computing, and X+CS -- none of that is indexed here yet, mirroring how castandards.json excludes the CA framework's '9-12 Specialty' set.

standards.paraphrase: An algorithm can hold onto more than one kind of information at once -- a number, a name, a yes/no flag -- and using several data types together is what lets it actually solve a problem or express an idea.
standards.scope_note: The expectation is designing and explaining the logic in words, a diagram, or pseudocode, not writing a program that runs, managing memory, or building data structures like lists or dictionaries.
practices: Computational Thinking: 6. Define computational problems.
Computational Thinking: 7. Develop and use abstractions.

standards.paraphrase: A flowchart or pseudocode can model someone else's algorithm, showing not just the sequence and branching but where a reusable, named procedure fits into it.
standards.scope_note: Modeling a given algorithm is the task -- designing or optimizing one, or converting the model into runnable code, isn't expected.
practices: Computational Thinking: 7. Develop and use abstractions.
Computational Thinking: 8. Create computing technologies.

standards.paraphrase: Checking whether an algorithm actually gives the right answer means tracing it, or running it, against specific inputs and comparing the result to what was expected.
standards.scope_note: This is testing against sample inputs, not a formal proof of correctness or an efficiency comparison between algorithms.
practices: Computational Thinking: 9. Test and refine computing technologies.
Human-Centered Design: 11. Use iterative design processes.

standards.paraphrase: Some problems are best solved with a fixed set of steps, some by following rules, and some by learning from data -- and picking the right one, or combining them, is a choice worth defending.
standards.scope_note: Reasoning about which approach fits and why is the point, not implementing any of the approaches.
practices: Computational Thinking: 6. Define computational problems.

standards.paraphrase: An AI tool -- a chatbot, an image classifier -- can generate something that helps solve a computational problem, and using it well means judging what it produces rather than just accepting it.
standards.scope_note: Using and evaluating an existing AI tool's output is the expectation; training a model or explaining how one works internally is not.
practices: Computational Thinking: 8. Create computing technologies.
Human-Centered Design: 11. Use iterative design processes.

standards.paraphrase: Watching what goes into a machine learning model and what comes out of it is enough to form a reasonable, evidence-based guess about how it's making its classifications or predictions.
standards.scope_note: Forming a hypothesis from observed behavior is the task; explaining the model's internal workings is not.
practices: Computational Thinking: 7. Develop and use abstractions.
Computational Thinking: 9. Test and refine computing technologies.

standards.paraphrase: A machine learning model gets more accurate and less biased when the examples it's trained on are examined and improved -- adding what's missing, fixing what's overrepresented.
standards.scope_note: This stays a conceptual, testing-and-suggesting exercise; students aren't expected to build a model or actually retrain one themselves.
practices: Ethics & Social Responsibility: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.
Computational Thinking: 9. Test and refine computing technologies.

standards.paraphrase: A model card or similar documentation spells out what a machine learning model is actually good for and where it falls short -- its training data, its intended use, its risks -- and reading that critically is its own skill.
standards.scope_note: Reviewing documentation and observed behavior is the expectation; building a model or accessing proprietary training data is not.
practices: Ethics & Social Responsibility: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.
Inclusive Collaboration: 3. Communicate effectively about computing.

standards.paraphrase: A familiar app or website can be checked against human-centered design principles -- empathy, accessibility, fairness -- to see which ones it actually lives up to.
standards.scope_note: Analyzing an existing technology, and suggesting improvements, is the task; designing or building a full technology from scratch is not.
practices: Ethics & Social Responsibility: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.
Human-Centered Design: 10. Understand and involve diverse users in design decisions.

standards.paraphrase: Everyday tools -- a photo app, a voice assistant, a recommendation feed -- carry their own ethical issues and biases, and noticing them in familiar, concrete examples is the starting point for evaluating computing responsibly.
standards.scope_note: Identifying and explaining bias in plain terms is the goal; understanding neural networks or studying formal AI policy is not.
practices: Ethics & Social Responsibility: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.
Human-Centered Design: 10. Understand and involve diverse users in design decisions.

standards.paraphrase: An existing algorithm can be reworked -- adding a language option, diversifying a playlist generator -- specifically to make its outcomes fairer or more inclusive.
standards.scope_note: Proposing a conceptual modification, verbally or as a diagram, is the expectation, not designing a complex algorithm from scratch or applying formal fairness statistics.
practices: Ethics & Social Responsibility: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.
Human-Centered Design: 12. Design computing technologies that empower and inform users.

standards.paraphrase: Naming a repeated block of steps and turning it into a procedure is what makes code easier to read and reuse.
standards.scope_note: Recognizing the opportunity and creating a simple procedure is the task; procedures with parameters or return values, or large modular systems, are not expected.
practices: Computational Thinking: 7. Develop and use abstractions.
Computational Thinking: 8. Create computing technologies.

standards.paraphrase: Documentation -- looking up what a function does, searching an error message -- is a normal, expected part of writing and fixing a program.
standards.scope_note: Using teacher-provided or self-selected, grade-appropriate documentation is the expectation; reading professional-level docs is not.
practices: Inclusive Collaboration: 4. Manage computing projects.
Computational Thinking: 9. Test and refine computing technologies.

standards.paraphrase: Code, images, music, and text used in a project all belong to someone, and giving credit -- knowing the difference between learning from someone's work and copying it -- is part of making anything.
standards.scope_note: Basic attribution and ethical awareness are the goal; studying copyright law or licensing one's own code is not.
practices: Ethics & Social Responsibility: 2. Respect others' rights and dignity when creating computing technologies.
Inclusive Collaboration: 3. Communicate effectively about computing.

standards.paraphrase: Building a program with a partner goes better with real collaboration habits -- sharing ideas while planning, giving and taking feedback, working respectfully on shared tools.
standards.scope_note: Classroom-level teamwork practices are the expectation, not formal frameworks like Agile/Scrum or professional project-management software.
practices: Inclusive Collaboration: 4. Manage computing projects.
Computational Thinking: 8. Create computing technologies.

standards.paraphrase: A program that stores several kinds of data in variables -- numbers, text, true/false -- can update them, make decisions based on them, and repeat actions using them.
standards.scope_note: Working with individual variables (incrementing, accumulating, converting) is the scope; lists, dictionaries, and other data structures are not expected here.
practices: Computational Thinking: 7. Develop and use abstractions.
Computational Thinking: 8. Create computing technologies.

standards.paraphrase: Tracing through a piece of code -- watching what a loop repeats, what a conditional branches on, what a variable holds at each step, what a procedure does when it's called -- is how you show you actually understand what it does.
standards.scope_note: Tracing execution is the task; debugging the code, testing it, or analyzing procedures that take parameters or return values is not.
practices: Inclusive Collaboration: 3. Communicate effectively about computing.
Computational Thinking: 7. Develop and use abstractions.

standards.paraphrase: Code an AI tool generated still needs a human check -- do the functions it calls actually exist, does the logic hold up, is it readable -- before it's trusted.
standards.scope_note: Evaluating given AI-generated code is the task; generating code with AI themselves, or judging code beyond their own level, is not expected.
practices: Computational Thinking: 9. Test and refine computing technologies.
Human-Centered Design: 11. Use iterative design processes.

standards.paraphrase: Finishing a program means actually testing it -- checking inputs and outputs, isolating a procedure, giving and getting feedback in a code review -- and writing down what changed and why.
standards.scope_note: Simple, systematic techniques and basic commenting are the expectation; debugging software, unit-testing frameworks, and version control are not.
practices: Inclusive Collaboration: 4. Manage computing projects.
Computational Thinking: 9. Test and refine computing technologies.

standards.paraphrase: Real feedback from real users -- especially about what's hard to use or hard to access -- should actually change the next version of a program.
standards.scope_note: Incremental, awareness-driven improvement is the goal; formal accessibility audits or frameworks are not expected.
practices: Human-Centered Design: 10. Understand and involve diverse users in design decisions.
Human-Centered Design: 11. Use iterative design processes.

standards.paraphrase: How precise and how fine-grained data collection is changes how accurate it is, how much storage it needs, and how useful it ends up being -- and different situations call for different tradeoffs.
standards.scope_note: Comparing given examples, like step counts recorded by minute versus by day, is the task; actually collecting data at varying precision is not required.
practices: Inclusive Collaboration: 3. Communicate effectively about computing.
Computational Thinking: 7. Develop and use abstractions.

standards.paraphrase: Metadata -- a photo's timestamp and location, not the picture itself -- answers different questions than the data it describes, often without anyone deliberately adding it.
standards.scope_note: Explaining the distinction using tools like file properties or page source is the expectation; technical metadata standards or formats are not.
practices: Ethics & Social Responsibility: 2. Respect others' rights and dignity when creating computing technologies.
Inclusive Collaboration: 3. Communicate effectively about computing.

standards.paraphrase: A spreadsheet or similar tool can sort, filter, group, and summarize a structured dataset, and explaining why each operation was chosen is part of the skill.
standards.scope_note: Working with an existing, grade-level dataset is the scope; collecting data, cleaning messy data, or mastering the software itself is not required.
practices: Inclusive Collaboration: 3. Communicate effectively about computing.
Computational Thinking: 7. Develop and use abstractions.

standards.paraphrase: A dataset with missing or misformatted values can be fixed more than one way -- deleting incomplete records, reformatting, or leaving it as-is -- and each option trades off differently, including the risk of introducing new bias.
standards.scope_note: Evaluating options on a provided dataset is the task; there's no single 'correct' fix to pick, and building automated error-detection tools isn't expected.
practices: Computational Thinking: 9. Test and refine computing technologies.
Human-Centered Design: 11. Use iterative design processes.

standards.paraphrase: A spreadsheet or programming tool can surface a relationship between variables in a dataset, and that relationship can then be used to make a prediction worth checking for sense.
standards.scope_note: Using a tool to find the relationship and sanity-check the prediction is the scope; statistics beyond grade-level math standards is not expected.
practices: Inclusive Collaboration: 4. Manage computing projects.
Computational Thinking: 7. Develop and use abstractions.

standards.paraphrase: The same dataset can be turned into more than one visualization, and comparing them for clarity, accuracy, and accessibility shows how a design choice changes what a reader takes away.
standards.scope_note: Working from existing data and comparing designs is the task; using a particular computational tool isn't required.
practices: Human-Centered Design: 10. Understand and involve diverse users in design decisions.
Human-Centered Design: 11. Use iterative design processes.

standards.paraphrase: Summarizing a finished data investigation -- the original question, how the data was gathered and analyzed, where bias or limitations crept in -- shows the reasoning behind the conclusions, not just the conclusions themselves.
standards.scope_note: Reflecting on an investigation, their own or someone else's (even via interview), is the task; actually collecting new data is not required.
practices: Inclusive Collaboration: 5. Act responsibly in computing collaborations.
Computational Thinking: 6. Define computational problems.

standards.paraphrase: Letting an app collect personal data trades a real benefit, like personalization or free access, against a real risk, like lost privacy or reduced control over the data -- and where that data ends up governed can cross national borders.
standards.scope_note: Explaining these tradeoffs conceptually, including basic data-sovereignty ideas, is the goal; technical protections like encryption or specific laws like GDPR/COPPA are not.
practices: Inclusive Collaboration: 3. Communicate effectively about computing.
Inclusive Collaboration: 5. Act responsibly in computing collaborations.

standards.paraphrase: Every stage of working with data -- collecting it, processing it, analyzing it, presenting it -- involves a human choice, and those choices can unintentionally bias the data, distort the conclusions, or weaken a model trained on it.
standards.scope_note: Recognizing this in simple examples is the expectation; advanced statistics or the technical mechanics of AI training are not.
practices: Ethics & Social Responsibility: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.
Human-Centered Design: 12. Design computing technologies that empower and inform users.

standards.paraphrase: Choosing between computing systems means weighing storage, connectivity, and accessibility features against a user's actual needs -- and naming at least one societal, environmental, or ethical cost that comes with the choice.
standards.scope_note: Comparing systems at a feature level is the scope; detailed technical specs like processor architecture are not expected.
practices: Human-Centered Design: 10. Understand and involve diverse users in design decisions.
Human-Centered Design: 12. Design computing technologies that empower and inform users.

standards.paraphrase: Specialized computing devices -- a robot, a vehicle's control unit, a medical imaging machine, a farm sensor -- all use the same input/output/processing/storage pattern to get real industry work done.
standards.scope_note: Describing how a chosen device works at that level is the task; building or programming the device is not.
practices: Inclusive Collaboration: 3. Communicate effectively about computing.
Computational Thinking: 6. Define computational problems.

standards.paraphrase: Confidentiality, integrity, and availability each protect data in a different way, and seeing what breaks when one of them fails -- a leaked password, an altered grade, a blocked website -- is how the CIA triad becomes real instead of abstract.
standards.scope_note: Explaining the effects in relatable contexts like school accounts, gaming, or social media is the goal; professional security audits or deep cryptography are not.
practices: Inclusive Collaboration: 3. Communicate effectively about computing.
Human-Centered Design: 12. Design computing technologies that empower and inform users.

standards.paraphrase: Phishing, malware, ransomware, and social engineering all exploit some mix of human behavior and system weakness, and knowing basic defenses -- strong passwords, multifactor login, spotting suspicious activity -- is the practical response.
standards.scope_note: Identifying attack types and prevention strategies is the scope; actually testing network defenses or analyzing how malware is built is not.
practices: Inclusive Collaboration: 3. Communicate effectively about computing.
Computational Thinking: 6. Define computational problems.

standards.paraphrase: A message crossing a network gets split into packets, encoded, sent independently, and reassembled at the other end -- and things like congestion or bad hardware can cause packets to get lost along the way.
standards.scope_note: Modeling this process and naming causes of packet loss is the task; detailed protocols like TCP/IP or configuring real hardware are not.
practices: Computational Thinking: 6. Define computational problems.
Computational Thinking: 7. Develop and use abstractions.

standards.paraphrase: The internet keeps working because it's built from many interconnected devices each playing a role -- routers directing traffic, servers hosting data, clients requesting it -- with enough redundant paths that losing one piece doesn't break the whole thing.
standards.scope_note: A conceptual explanation of roles and resilience is the goal; configuring real networking equipment or explaining protocols in technical detail is not.
practices: Inclusive Collaboration: 3. Communicate effectively about computing.
Computational Thinking: 6. Define computational problems.

standards.paraphrase: Making a computing system genuinely usable by people with different needs -- captions, adjustable text, alternative input devices -- is something a team can propose and refine together, then test with peers.
standards.scope_note: Proposing and peer-testing design improvements is the task; building accessible hardware from scratch or professional usability testing is not.
practices: Inclusive Collaboration: 5. Act responsibly in computing collaborations.
Human-Centered Design: 12. Design computing technologies that empower and inform users.

standards.paraphrase: Access to computing isn't even -- income, physical ability, geography, and community resources like libraries or Wi-Fi hotspots all shape who actually gets to use a computing system.
standards.scope_note: Investigating examples of this digital divide, using provided data, maps, or local surveys, is the scope; large-scale statistical analysis or policy evaluation is not.
practices: Inclusive Collaboration: 3. Communicate effectively about computing.
Human-Centered Design: 10. Understand and involve diverse users in design decisions.

standards.paraphrase: Individuals, communities, companies, and governments have all shaped computing technology differently across its history -- designing it, funding it, regulating it, using it -- and they often influenced or worked with each other.
standards.scope_note: Comparing these roles with described examples is the task; memorizing timelines or ranking groups by importance is not.
practices: Inclusive Collaboration: 3. Communicate effectively about computing.
Human-Centered Design: 10. Understand and involve diverse users in design decisions.

standards.paraphrase: A computing technology's original purpose and its actual, unintended effects on society and the environment -- on communication, jobs, privacy, e-waste, energy use -- are two different things worth tracing separately.
standards.scope_note: Simple cause-and-effect connections are the expectation; formal cost-benefit analysis or predicting future technology is not.
practices: Ethics & Social Responsibility: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.
Inclusive Collaboration: 5. Act responsibly in computing collaborations.

standards.paraphrase: An emerging technology like AI, robotics, or quantum computing is only worth using on a given problem if its actual capabilities, reliability, and environmental cost make sense for that problem right now.
standards.scope_note: Judging appropriateness from known capabilities and limits is the task; explaining the underlying mechanics or predicting future breakthroughs is not.
practices: Ethics & Social Responsibility: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.
Human-Centered Design: 10. Understand and involve diverse users in design decisions.

standards.paraphrase: The design choices behind a new technology -- what languages it supports, what it costs, what connectivity it assumes -- create real benefits for some communities and real barriers for others.
standards.scope_note: Evaluating examples through one or more of those factors is the scope; formal usability studies or building prototypes are not.
practices: Ethics & Social Responsibility: 2. Respect others' rights and dignity when creating computing technologies.
Inclusive Collaboration: 3. Communicate effectively about computing.

standards.paraphrase: Whether an emerging technology helps or harms a local community is a genuinely debatable question, and building an argued, evidence-backed case for one side is the point.
standards.scope_note: A researched debate on a specific technology's community impact is the task; deep technical understanding of the technology itself is not required.
practices: Ethics & Social Responsibility: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.
Computational Thinking: 8. Create computing technologies.

standards.paraphrase: It's the human decisions behind a computing system -- what data got collected, which algorithm got used, how results got interpreted -- that actually create its ethical and social consequences, not the technology by itself.
standards.scope_note: Tracing those human choices to their effects, and proposing more responsible alternatives, is the task; philosophical debates about AI consciousness or rights are not.
practices: Ethics & Social Responsibility: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.
Computational Thinking: 6. Define computational problems.

standards.paraphrase: The same computational thinking moves -- breaking a problem down, spotting a pattern, abstracting a solution -- that students use while coding show up in how professionals in very different fields actually solve problems.
standards.scope_note: Drawing that parallel through described examples is the scope; specialized programming frameworks or domain-specific simulations are not expected.
practices: Inclusive Collaboration: 4. Manage computing projects.
Computational Thinking: 6. Define computational problems.

standards.paraphrase: Automation -- robotics, AI, machine learning -- reshapes work by making some tasks faster or safer while displacing or changing others, and weighing those tradeoffs is part of understanding its impact.
standards.scope_note: Exploring examples of both benefit and disruption is the goal; designing automated systems or doing formal economic or labor-market analysis is not.
practices: Ethics & Social Responsibility: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.
Computational Thinking: 6. Define computational problems.

standards.paraphrase: Solving a problem well often means choosing the right data structure to go with the algorithm, not just writing steps in isolation.
standards.scope_note: The focus is picking and using structures a language already provides (like a list or a class) to support the plan, not implementing custom structures from scratch -- a leaderboard built on a list plus a sort is the kind of example this covers.
practices: Computational Thinking: 7. Develop and use abstractions.
Computational Thinking: 9. Test and refine computing technologies.

standards.paraphrase: An algorithm can be reworked to run more clearly or efficiently by wrapping repeated steps in a function and using loops or conditionals instead of restating logic.
standards.scope_note: This is about restructuring code with existing constructs like functions and loops, not formal efficiency analysis or advanced recursive optimization.
practices: Computational Thinking: 6. Define computational problems.
Computational Thinking: 7. Develop and use abstractions.

standards.paraphrase: Comparing two algorithms for the same job means checking more than just whether they work -- how fast they run and how easy they are to read matter too.
standards.scope_note: Comparisons can be informal or based on test runs rather than a formal proof of running time.
practices: Computational Thinking: 9. Test and refine computing technologies.

standards.paraphrase: An algorithm that always gives the same result from the same input behaves differently from one that leans on randomness and can vary run to run.
standards.scope_note: Explaining the distinction in plain terms is enough; formal probability calculations aren't expected.
practices: Computational Thinking: 6. Define computational problems.

standards.paraphrase: Content that comes out of an AI tool -- text, an image, even code -- deserves a critical look for whether it's accurate, skewed, or capable of causing harm.
standards.scope_note: The judgment call is about the output itself, not about understanding how the model that produced it works internally.
practices: Ethics & Social Responsibility: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.
Computational Thinking: 9. Test and refine computing technologies.

standards.paraphrase: Picking one kind of AI approach over another for a task is a decision that should be defended, weighing things like how much data there is and how easy the result is for a person to interpret.
standards.scope_note: The point is arguing for a choice between approaches, not building or deriving the math behind them.
practices: Inclusive Collaboration: 3. Communicate effectively about computing.
Computational Thinking: 7. Develop and use abstractions.

standards.paraphrase: Before trusting a dataset, it's worth asking where it came from, how complete and accurate it is, whether it represents everyone it should, and whether using it raises privacy concerns.
standards.scope_note: This is a critical-eyes evaluation, not a statistical proof of bias or a formal correction procedure.
practices: Ethics & Social Responsibility: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.
Ethics & Social Responsibility: 2. Respect others' rights and dignity when creating computing technologies.

standards.paraphrase: Building a working machine-learning model for a specific job means choosing suitable data and tools, training it, and checking whether it actually performs the task.
standards.scope_note: Using an existing tool or simple library to build and test the model is the expectation, not writing the learning algorithm from scratch.
practices: Computational Thinking: 8. Create computing technologies.
Computational Thinking: 9. Test and refine computing technologies.

standards.paraphrase: Designing something so that it's genuinely usable by a wide range of people means researching what those people need and thinking ahead about a design's social and ethical side effects.
standards.scope_note: Considering accessibility law and practical inclusive-design choices (contrast, navigation, plain language) is the expectation, not meeting every clause of a formal accessibility standard.
practices: Computational Thinking: 8. Create computing technologies.
Human-Centered Design: 10. Understand and involve diverse users in design decisions.

standards.paraphrase: Both an algorithm built from explicit rules and one trained on data can end up treating people unfairly, and tracing where that unfairness comes from is part of evaluating it responsibly.
standards.scope_note: The analysis stays conceptual -- recognizing patterns of bias and suggesting fixes -- rather than auditing a real company's system or running statistics on it.
practices: Ethics & Social Responsibility: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.
Computational Thinking: 9. Test and refine computing technologies.

standards.paraphrase: Every algorithmic system's design quietly favors some outcomes over others, and naming which values -- efficiency, privacy, fairness -- got prioritized is part of understanding it.
standards.scope_note: The goal is identifying the priorities baked into a design, not reverse-engineering a real company's business model.
practices: Ethics & Social Responsibility: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.
Human-Centered Design: 10. Understand and involve diverse users in design decisions.

standards.paraphrase: Splitting a program into distinct, well-organized pieces -- functions, imported libraries, or objects -- makes the result easier to read and easier to reuse.
standards.scope_note: Straightforward decomposition is the target; elaborate design patterns or deep class hierarchies aren't expected.
practices: Computational Thinking: 7. Develop and use abstractions.
Computational Thinking: 8. Create computing technologies.

standards.paraphrase: Good program development leans on outside resources -- reference docs, existing libraries, simple APIs, and the features built into a development environment -- rather than reinventing everything from scratch.
standards.scope_note: Using these resources well is the goal, not building new ones.
practices: Ethics & Social Responsibility: 2. Respect others' rights and dignity when creating computing technologies.
Computational Thinking: 9. Test and refine computing technologies.

standards.paraphrase: Anything borrowed from someone else -- code, art, sound -- needs to be credited according to whatever terms it was shared under.
standards.scope_note: Practicing honest attribution is the point, not mastering copyright law itself.
practices: Ethics & Social Responsibility: 2. Respect others' rights and dignity when creating computing technologies.
Inclusive Collaboration: 3. Communicate effectively about computing.

standards.paraphrase: Working on a program as a team goes better with some structure -- assigned roles, a shared design document, and a way to track who changed what.
standards.scope_note: Classroom-scale tools and practices are the expectation, not professional-grade project management.
practices: Inclusive Collaboration: 4. Manage computing projects.
Inclusive Collaboration: 5. Act responsibly in computing collaborations.

standards.paraphrase: Choosing the right structure -- a list, a dictionary -- to hold a program's data is what makes storing, retrieving, and changing that data manageable.
standards.scope_note: Common built-in structures are the scope here; things like linked lists, trees, and graphs are not.
practices: Computational Thinking: 7. Develop and use abstractions.
Computational Thinking: 8. Create computing technologies.

standards.paraphrase: Reading someone else's code well means being able to explain what each moving part does -- a variable holding state, a loop repeating until some condition, a conditional branching on it -- and how those parts cooperate.
standards.scope_note: This is about tracing a manageable segment of code, not untangling a large system with many interacting structures.
practices: Computational Thinking: 6. Define computational problems.
Computational Thinking: 7. Develop and use abstractions.

standards.paraphrase: Code that an AI tool produces still has to be tested against what it was actually supposed to do, including checking that it holds up on tricky or edge-case inputs.
standards.scope_note: The task is testing and judging the output, not understanding the model that generated it.
practices: Computational Thinking: 6. Define computational problems.
Computational Thinking: 9. Test and refine computing technologies.

standards.paraphrase: Finishing a program includes checking it against its own original plan -- does it work correctly, does it do what it was meant to, and is it actually pleasant and accessible to use.
standards.scope_note: This is a self- or peer-review against the project's own stated goals, not a formal verification process or industry tooling.
practices: Computational Thinking: 9. Test and refine computing technologies.
Human-Centered Design: 11. Use iterative design processes.

standards.paraphrase: Feedback and test results should actually change the program -- tightening up usability, accessibility, or accuracy -- even if not every issue gets fixed at once.
standards.scope_note: Meaningful, partial improvement is the expectation, not chasing full optimization or fixing every possible issue.
practices: Human-Centered Design: 10. Understand and involve diverse users in design decisions.
Human-Centered Design: 11. Use iterative design processes.

standards.paraphrase: A simulation often needs input data that doesn't exist yet, and a simple program or spreadsheet formula can manufacture data meeting whatever constraints the simulation calls for.
standards.scope_note: Producing the data that feeds into an existing simulation is the task, not building the simulation itself.
practices: Computational Thinking: 8. Create computing technologies.
Human-Centered Design: 12. Design computing technologies that empower and inform users.

standards.paraphrase: A data dictionary spells out, for every column in a dataset, its name, its type, and the values it's allowed to hold -- plus how columns depend on each other, like a skipped survey question leaving a related answer blank.
standards.scope_note: Documenting an existing dataset this way is the task; building the dataset, or handling huge or specialized data, is not.
practices: Computational Thinking: 7. Develop and use abstractions.
Computational Thinking: 8. Create computing technologies.

standards.paraphrase: Messy text data -- inconsistent capitalization, typos, a name and a date crammed into one field -- usually needs cleanup before it's useful, and a spreadsheet or short script can do that work.
standards.scope_note: Recognizing where a pattern-matching tool like a regular expression would help is part of this; building a cleaning tool from scratch, or handling huge unstructured feeds, is not.
practices: Computational Thinking: 9. Test and refine computing technologies.
Human-Centered Design: 11. Use iterative design processes.

standards.paraphrase: There's more than one way to check that a dataset's values are the right type and fall in a sensible range, and weighing those approaches against each other is its own skill.
standards.scope_note: Comparing validation approaches conceptually is the expectation; writing the validation code or using statistical models is not.
practices: Computational Thinking: 6. Define computational problems.
Computational Thinking: 7. Develop and use abstractions.

standards.paraphrase: Turning a dataset with several variables into a chart -- a scatter plot, a stacked bar chart -- is how a question about that data gets answered visually.
standards.scope_note: Using existing tools like spreadsheets to build the visualization is the expectation, not writing code to generate it or running formal statistics.
practices: Inclusive Collaboration: 4. Manage computing projects.
Computational Thinking: 8. Create computing technologies.

standards.paraphrase: A chart or simulation someone else built can still mislead -- a truncated axis, a biased sample -- and spotting those limits is as important as reading the result itself.
standards.scope_note: Critiquing an existing data product is the task, not building one or fixing the code behind it.
practices: Ethics & Social Responsibility: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.

standards.paraphrase: Collecting and processing data at scale carries real costs beyond the technical -- consent, who owns the data, bias baked into it, misinformation, even the environmental footprint of the data centers running it.
standards.scope_note: The analysis is conceptual, not a formal legal or economic study of data policy.
practices: Ethics & Social Responsibility: 2. Respect others' rights and dignity when creating computing technologies.

standards.paraphrase: Whether an existing data-privacy law or policy actually works is a debatable question, and building an argument on either side -- including whether public pressure or behavior change might work better than a new law -- is the point.
standards.scope_note: Debating the policy's effectiveness is the expectation; reading the actual legal text is not.
practices: Ethics & Social Responsibility: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.

standards.paraphrase: An operating system stands apart from ordinary software because its job is managing the machine itself -- memory, storage, whatever's plugged in -- so other programs can just run.
standards.scope_note: Describing that role is the goal, not learning how an operating system is actually coded or configuring its internals.
practices: Inclusive Collaboration: 3. Communicate effectively about computing.

standards.paraphrase: Putting a real device to work on some everyday task also means noticing what it can't do -- battery life, screen size, and other limits that come with the choice.
standards.scope_note: Using a device thoughtfully is the expectation, not building one or writing code that controls its hardware directly.

standards.paraphrase: Every security measure protects something at some cost -- multifactor login guards an account but makes it slower to get into -- and naming that trade-off is part of understanding security.
standards.scope_note: Recognizing these trade-offs conceptually is the goal, not implementing the security measures.
practices: Ethics & Social Responsibility: 2. Respect others' rights and dignity when creating computing technologies.

standards.paraphrase: The same security breach can hit different groups in different ways -- a person's identity, a company's finances, a whole community's trust in a system -- and sorting out who's affected and how is more than just listing consequences.
standards.scope_note: This is broad-impact analysis, not a forensic investigation or professional-grade tooling.
practices: Ethics & Social Responsibility: 2. Respect others' rights and dignity when creating computing technologies.

standards.paraphrase: Given a described security weakness, proposing a fix means naming the vulnerability, what could go wrong because of it, and concrete steps -- technical and non-technical -- to close the gap.
standards.scope_note: Proposing the fix is the task; actually building it is not.
practices: Ethics & Social Responsibility: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.

standards.paraphrase: A network diagram shows both the physical pieces -- servers, routers, devices -- and the software running on them, and how all of it connects to get work done.
standards.scope_note: Drawing the diagram is the task, not physically building the network.

standards.paraphrase: The internet is really a network stitched together out of many smaller networks, with its own layered structure, hardware like routers, and protocols like TCP/IP tying it together -- which sets it apart from something like a single classroom network.
standards.scope_note: A high-level, conceptual grasp is the goal, not configuring real equipment or analyzing network traffic.
practices: Computational Thinking: 7. Develop and use abstractions.

standards.paraphrase: Laws and policies about how computing systems get built and used usually exist for a reason -- technical, legal, or social -- and explaining that reasoning matters more than reciting the rule.
standards.scope_note: Understanding why a policy exists is the point; reading the legal text itself is not.

standards.paraphrase: Computing infrastructure has a physical life cycle -- energy-hungry data centers, e-waste, supply chains -- and those costs don't land on everyone equally, which makes asking who's affected and why part of the investigation.
standards.scope_note: Researching and explaining the impact is the task, not proposing a technical fix for it.
practices: Ethics & Social Responsibility: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.

standards.paraphrase: Tracing a technology's history from its start to now usually turns up moments where forces outside the technology itself -- economics, culture, politics -- pushed its design or adoption in a particular direction.
standards.scope_note: Working from reliable secondary sources is the expectation, not original historical research or deep economic modeling.
practices: Ethics & Social Responsibility: 1. Use computing for positive social impact.

standards.paraphrase: A privacy law or a rule about algorithmic transparency exists to head off some specific harm, and being able to explain that reasoning is what this is really about.
standards.scope_note: Explaining the reasoning behind a policy is the point, not drafting legal language or mastering the lawmaking process.

standards.paraphrase: An emerging technology usually does something genuinely different under the hood, and that difference is what lets it do new things or get past an old limitation.
standards.scope_note: How deep the technical explanation goes depends on the topic and the students -- the underlying advanced theory isn't required.

standards.paraphrase: A new technology's upside rarely lands evenly -- weighing its benefits against its costs means asking who gets left out of the access or the outcomes.
standards.scope_note: A reasoned, conceptual argument is the goal, not a formal data-driven study.

standards.paraphrase: Sketching out how an emerging technology could tackle a real problem means backing the idea with real research and being honest about who might be helped or harmed by it.

standards.paraphrase: The people behind a computing system -- the ones who chose its data, tuned it, decided how it gets used -- make choices that carry their own risks and benefits down the line.
standards.scope_note: Tracing those human choices and their consequences is the focus, not building or mathematically analyzing the underlying model.

standards.paraphrase: Whether an AI system could ever be intelligent the way a person is opens real philosophical questions about consciousness and who's responsible for what it does.
standards.scope_note: This is a debate about ideas, not an exploration of neuroscience or a specific model's architecture.

standards.paraphrase: Looking at how real, varied computing professionals actually work -- the problems they run into, the barriers they've navigated -- connects computational thinking back to the people who practice it.
